lines.text: it is this very conception which Jesus opposes, and He
wishes to replace it by a different understanding of God.
And what is His conception? Just that of God's sovereign
freedom. God is free over against all human claims! "I
choose to give to this last as I give to you. Am I not allowed
to do what I choose with what belongs to me?" says the
householder in the parable, and the remark is intended to
illustrate God's absolute freedom. Man must bow before the
transcendence of this divine freedom and not ask why. God
is sovereignly free and unfettered by human claims; and
whoever dares to speak of God or to reckon with God must
be clear about this. Man is subject to the free will of God and
has no right to make claims against God.
Thus far our parable teaches us nothing other than the
parable about the master and his slaves. But it does not teach
us this lesson alone; there is something decisively important
which it adds. What is the real sting of the offence which
the grumbling workmen feel? They are not of course
offended because they have been badly treated, because
their pay has been reduced or kept back. The sting lies rather
in the fact that the others who have worked less than
themselves receive none the less the same reward. And on
what grounds does it rest that the employer gives these
latter the same recompense? On the grounds of his sheer
kindness and generosity. He shames the grumblers by his
question: "Do you begrudge my generosity?" Did not they
whom no one had hired need a day's wages just as much as
they who were first hired? Were they not also men who
suffered hunger and thirst? Did they not likewise want
money for the needs of their life and of their families? Were
they to be made to suffer because up to evening they had
found no remunerative work?
